latin.366: CAPUT VII. Examen trium similitudinum, quibus imputatio primi peccati actualis Adami illustratur eodem Cap. IV. Tu tandem infamem tuam imputationem illustrare quibusdam similitudinibus, ac quodam probabilitatis fuco oblinire niteris, quas expendere est animus, & ostendere quam ei non faveant. Primam sumis ab aulico Regis amico, qui infidelitatis & laesae-majestatis reus privatur titulis, dignitatibus, & fundis, quos sibi & suis acquisiverat. Nunquid enim, inquis, verum est potuisse sibi & posteris haec omnia servare, modo fidelis sit? Infidelitas ergo sive patris, sive avi, toti familiae obfuit. Et, si posteri considerentur illis bonis exuti, & infames facti, nonne dicitur delictum illius causa esse bonorum perditorum, & infamiae, & toti familiae imputatum? nam sicut sibi toti familiae acceperat sub conditione, sic in conditionem peccans tota familia in illo peccavit & cecidit.
latin.367: Haec similitudo misere claudicat. Primum conditio est fidelitas; bona tituli, dignitates, fundi. Itaque conditio, & bona sub illa conditione accepta sunt res admodum diversae, & natura sua separabiles. Possunt enim bona illa bello, vel profusione, vel alea, vel litibus temere susceptis, vel aliqua alia re amitti conservata fide, aut hac violata retineri. Hic vero bona sunt rectitudo, justitia, sanctitas, conditio horum ipsorum bonorum conservatio. Quid enim ab Adamo exigebatur nisi ut perseveraret in rectitudine, justitia, sanctitate, fide, officio? Annon haec ipsa bona fidem includunt? obedientiam Deo continent.
latin.368: Quaenam autem fuit conditionis violatio, quod peccatum Adami? infidelitas, inobedientia, ambitio, superbia, ingratitudo, cupedia, curiositas, a Deo aversio, ad creaturas conversio &c. quae, quomodo cum perfecta rectitudine, justitia, sanctitate, innocentia consistere potuerint, equidem intelligere non possum. Hinc aliud nascitur discrimen, nam violata fide, ut bonis a Rege acceptis Aulicus privetur, opus est Regis, vel judicis actione, nempe judicio, & judicii executione. Alioqui tituli illi, dignitates, & fundi retinerentur ab Aulico.
latin.369: Adamus vero violata fide factus a Deo apostata, Deo rebellis, non potuit amplius integer, justus, sanctus, rectus, bonus esse: nec ut privaretur justitia & rectitudine ullo Dei judicio, ulla actione judiciaria opus fuit: hoc ipso quod lapsus est desiit esse in eo, in quo collocatus fuerat, gradu: hoc ipso quod se a fine ultimo vero ad falso apparentem intorsit & incurvavit, desiit rectus esse, hoc ipso quod suum Deo jus reddere noluit infidelis & rebellis creatori suo & domino optimo, desiit justus esse.
latin.370: GAR. Respondeo 1. nihil hic opus esse singularibus eiusmodi similitudinis capitibus; dummodo id obtineamus hoc exemplo, non esse quod putent homines, doctrinam de imputatione primi peccati continere aliquid, quod merito habendum sit pro absono aut iniquo. Cur enim decreto Dei injustitiam adscribant, qui judicum humanorum decretis in causa perduellionis non adscribunt? Eo impetrato, parum interest ad causam quae nunc agitur, secusne habeat, necne, imputatio peccati Adae, quam imputatio peccati perduellium. Nec vero nos ii sumus, qui putemus esse in utraque omnia similia. PLAC. Si de imputatione primi peccati mediata loquitur, facile doceam nihil continere absoni aut iniqui. Sin de immediata, nego id posse hoc exemplo obtineri, cum sit admodum dissimile, & quidem ea dissimilitudine, qua maxime ad rem facit de qua agitur.
latin.371: GAR. Secundo, quanquam in explicatione illa dissimilitudinum est, quod merito desideremus. Primum enim cum quatuor proposita fuerint, de bonis separabilibus, de aliis modis amittendi, de judicis decreto, de filiis nascentibus & nepotibus: tamen ubi dissimilitudinis capita explicantur, de primo membro nihil dicitur. Bona, inquis, perduellis sunt separabilia natura sua. Quid igitur? Et bona Adami, quae pro se, & suis acceperat, non erant ab ipso separabilia natura sua? Imo non separabilia tantum fuerunt, sed & actu separata sunt, quippe amissa per primam illam inobedientiam. Ergo in hoc frustra dissimilitudo statuitur.

pass_a.366: Cap. VII opens Placeus's exam of three similitudes by which GAR illustrates imputing Adam's first actual sin (same Cap. IV). Placeus will weigh them and show they do not favor that imputation. First similitude: a courtier friend of the King, guilty of unfaithfulness and lese-majesty, stripped of titles, dignities, and estates gotten for himself and his—so the father's or grandfather's unfaithfulness harms the whole family, and the delict is said imputed to them as cause of lost goods and infamy, since he received under condition for the whole house.
pass_a.367: Placeus: the similitude limps. Condition is faithfulness; goods are titles, dignities, estates—diverse and by nature separable. Those goods can be lost while faith is kept, or kept while faith is broken (war, dice, lawsuits, etc.). In Adam the 'goods' are rectitude, justice, holiness, and the condition is conserving those very goods. What Adam owed was perseverance in rectitude, justice, holiness, faith, duty—goods that already include faith and contain obedience to God.
pass_a.368: Adam's sin—the condition's breach—was unfaithfulness, disobedience, pride, aversion from God, conversion to creatures, and the rest, which cannot stand with perfect rectitude, justice, holiness, innocence. Another difference: to strip the courtier of royal gifts after broken faith needs the King's or a judge's act—judgment and execution—or else he keeps titles, dignities, and estates.
pass_a.369: Adam, faith broken, becomes apostate and rebel and can no longer be integral, just, holy, upright, good. No divine judgment or judicial action is needed to deprive him of justice and rectitude: by falling he leaves his grade; by twisting from the true last end to a false one he ceases to be upright; by refusing God his right as unfaithful rebel he ceases to be just.
pass_a.370: GAR answers first that Placeus's singular dissimilar heads are unnecessary if the courtier example only shows men need not think first-sin imputation absurd or iniquitous—why ascribe injustice to God's decree when they do not ascribe it to human judges' decrees in treason cases? Once that is won, whether Adam's imputation matches traitors' in every point matters little; GAR does not claim total likeness. Placeus: if the talk is of mediate first-sin imputation, nothing absurd or inequitable; if immediate, this example cannot obtain it, being exceedingly unlike—and by the very unlikeness that most bears on the present quarrel.
pass_a.371: GAR's second complaint: Placeus listed four dissimilarity heads—separable goods, other ways of losing, the judge's decree, sons being born and grandsons—yet when he explained the dissimilarities he said nothing of the first member. If a traitor's goods are separable by their nature, were not Adam's goods which he received for himself and his also separable—and in fact actually separated, lost by that first disobedience? So in this the dissimilarity is set up in vain. Tip into Placeus's reply on what 'separable' meant.

366: CAPUT VII. Examination of three similitudes by which the imputation of Adam's first actual sin is illustrated in the same Cap. IV. You at length try to illustrate your infamous imputation by certain similitudes, and to smear it with a certain paint of probability, which it is my mind to weigh and to show how little they favor it. The first you take from a courtier friend of the King who, guilty of unfaithfulness and lese-majesty, is deprived of titles, dignities, and estates which he had acquired for himself and his. For is it not true, you ask, that he could have kept all these for himself and his posterity, provided he were faithful? Therefore the unfaithfulness either of the father or of the grandfather harmed the whole family. And if the posterity are considered stripped of those goods and made infamous, is not that delict said to be the cause of the lost goods and of the infamy, and imputed to the whole family? for just as he had received for himself and the whole family under a condition, so in sinning against the condition the whole family sinned and fell in him.
367: This similitude limps miserably. First, the condition is faithfulness; the goods are titles, dignities, estates. And so the condition, and the goods received under that condition, are things altogether diverse and by their nature separable. For those goods can be lost by war, or prodigality, or dice, or lawsuits rashly undertaken, or some other thing, while faith is kept—or, faith being violated, can be retained. Here, however, the goods are rectitude, justice, holiness; the condition is the conservation of these very goods. For what was required of Adam except that he persevere in rectitude, justice, holiness, faith, duty? Do not these very goods include faith? do they not contain obedience to God?
368: But what was the violation of the condition—Adam's sin? unfaithfulness, disobedience, ambition, pride, ingratitude, greed, curiosity, aversion from God, conversion to creatures, &c.—which, how they could have stood with perfect rectitude, justice, holiness, innocence, I for my part cannot understand. Hence another difference is born: for faith being violated, that the Courtier be deprived of the goods received from the King, there is need of the King's or a judge's action, namely judgment and execution of judgment. Otherwise those titles, dignities, and estates would be retained by the Courtier.
369: But Adam, faith being violated, made an apostate from God and a rebel against God, could no longer be integral, just, holy, upright, or good. Nor was any judgment of God, or any judicial action, needed for him to be deprived of justice and rectitude. By this very thing—that he fell—he ceased to be in the grade in which he had been placed. By this very thing—that he twisted and bent himself from the true last end to a falsely apparent one—he ceased to be upright. By this very thing—that unwilling to render God his right he became unfaithful and a rebel to his creator and best lord—he ceased to be just.
370: GAR. I answer first: there is no need here of such singular heads of the similitude; provided only we obtain by this example that men need not think the doctrine of the imputation of the first sin contains anything that is deservedly to be held absurd or iniquitous. For why should they ascribe injustice to God's decree who do not ascribe it to human judges' decrees in a case of treason? That being obtained, it matters little to the cause now treated whether Adam's sin-imputation stands otherwise than the traitors' sin-imputation or not. Nor are we those who think everything in both is alike. PLAC. If he speaks of a mediate imputation of the first sin, I can easily teach that it contains nothing absurd or iniquitous. But if of an immediate, I deny that can be obtained by this example, since it is exceedingly unlike—and by that very unlikeness which most of all bears on the matter treated.
371: GAR. Second, although in that explanation of dissimilarities there is what we may deservedly desire. For first, though four things were proposed—concerning separable goods, concerning other ways of losing, concerning the judge's decree, concerning sons being born and grandsons—yet when the heads of dissimilarity are explained, nothing is said of the first member. The goods, you say, of the traitor are separable by their nature. What then? And Adam's goods, which he had received for himself and his, were they not separable from him by their nature? Nay, they were not only separable, but were actually separated, seeing they were lost by that first disobedience. Therefore in this the dissimilarity is set up in vain.
